--- title: "Missing values and outliers" description: "What to do with missing and unusual values once you have found them, and why each fix depends on knowing why the value is missing or strange." order: 5 categories: [data-preparation, marine-data] --- ## Every quick fix can do damage Every fix for missing or unusual values has a default, and each default sometimes does damage. Dropping incomplete rows can quietly delete much of a season; filling gaps with the average invents data nobody measured; removing outliers erases real extreme events. This page shows how to choose a fix by asking first why a value is missing or strange, and applies that to the problems [Exploring the data first](exploratory-analysis.qmd) found in the raw survey file. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Ask why before fixing A value can be missing for three kinds of reason, and a value can look unusual for three kinds of reason. Each needs a different response: ::: {.diagram} ![Three reasons a value can be missing and three reasons a value can look unusual, with what to do in each case. Only the first kind of missing value is harmless, and only the first kind of unusual value is safe to remove.](img/missing-and-unusual.svg){fig-alt="Two rows of three cards. Why is it missing: completely at random, unrelated to anything, such as a dropped sample, where dropping costs only precision; at random, depending on something recorded, such as more gaps in winter, where you fill in from what was recorded; not at random, depending on the missing value itself, such as a sensor failing in storms, where no data fix exists and you must know the instrument. Why is it unusual: impossible, such as a salinity of minus 999, to correct or mark missing; a genuine extreme, such as a spawning aggregation, to keep; a plausible error, such as a depth ten times too deep that still looks normal, which cannot be found."} ::: The names are statisticians' and not very clear. **Missing at random** means the gaps follow something you *did* record: the survey's chlorophyll is missing most often in winter, and the season is in the table. Filling those gaps from the recorded columns can undo much of the damage. But ask why winter values are missing. If cloud blocked the sensor, and cloud also lowers chlorophyll, then the gaps depend on the missing values themselves, and nothing in the data can repair that. Far from the average is not the same as wrong. A rule such as "more than three standard deviations from the mean" finds rare values, and in marine counts the rare values are often the real and important ones. Remove a value only when you can say what is wrong with it. ## Sentinels become missing values The `-999` values mean "missing", so they are converted to `NA`, R's code for a missing value, after removing the duplicated rows: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} raw <- load_coastal_survey_raw() clean <- raw |> distinct() |> mutate( salinity_psu = na_if(salinity_psu, -999), temperature_c = na_if(temperature_c, -999) ) clean |> summarise(across(c(temperature_c, salinity_psu, chlorophyll_mg_m3), list(missing = \(x) sum(is.na(x)), mean = \(x) round(mean(x, na.rm = TRUE), 2)))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| temperature_c_missing| temperature_c_mean| salinity_psu_missing| salinity_psu_mean| chlorophyll_mg_m3_missing| chlorophyll_mg_m3_mean| |---------------------:|------------------:|--------------------:|-----------------:|-------------------------:|----------------------:| | 8| 8.63| 24| 33.92| 51| 1.43|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_raw raw = load_coastal_survey_raw() clean = raw.drop_duplicates().copy() clean["salinity_psu"] = clean["salinity_psu"].replace(-999, np.nan) clean["temperature_c"] = clean["temperature_c"].replace(-999, np.nan) columns = ["temperature_c", "salinity_psu", "chlorophyll_mg_m3"] pd.DataFrame({ "missing": clean[columns].isna().sum(), "mean": clean[columns].mean().round(2), # pandas skips NaN, as na.rm does }) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | | missing | mean | |:------------------|----------:|-------:| | temperature_c | 8 | 8.63 | | salinity_psu | 24 | 33.92 | | chlorophyll_mg_m3 | 51 | 1.43 | ::: ::: ::: Salinity's mean moves from 2.24 to 33.9. The values are still missing, but now honestly so, and no summary is dragged towards −999 any more. ## Categories are standardised ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} clean <- clean |> mutate(substrate = str_to_lower(str_trim(substrate)), substrate = fct_collapse(substrate, sand = c("sand", "sandy"), mud = c("mud", "muddy"), gravel = "gravel", rock = c("rock", "rocky"))) count(clean, substrate) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|substrate | n| |:---------|---:| |gravel | 139| |mud | 303| |rock | 55| |sand | 303|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} substrate = clean["substrate"].str.strip().str.lower() clean["substrate"] = substrate.replace( {"sandy": "sand", "muddy": "mud", "rocky": "rock"} ) clean["substrate"].value_counts().reset_index() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | substrate | count | |:------------|--------:| | mud | 303 | | sand | 303 | | gravel | 139 | | rock | 55 | ::: ::: ::: That code contains a judgement. Is `sandy` the same as `sand`, or was one observer recording "sandy mud"? Here they are merged; on a real survey, ask whoever recorded them. ## Impossible depths are corrected ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} clean |> filter(depth_m > 250) |> select(station_id, depth_m, temperature_c) |> arrange(desc(depth_m)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|station_id | depth_m| temperature_c| |:----------|-------:|-------------:| |ST0054 | 1581| 3.11| |ST0584 | 1463| 11.04| |ST0284 | 1392| 6.19| |ST0145 | 1335| 10.50| |ST0677 | 1174| 8.34| |ST0129 | 1052| 8.21| |ST0202 | 1051| 5.05| |ST0344 | 808| 7.96| |ST0167 | 629| 10.09| |ST0655 | 283| 8.33|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} (clean.loc[clean["depth_m"] > 250, ["station_id", "depth_m", "temperature_c"]] .sort_values("depth_m", ascending=False)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | | station_id | depth_m | temperature_c | |----:|:-------------|----------:|----------------:| | 423 | ST0054 | 1581 | 3.11 | | 286 | ST0584 | 1463 | 11.04 | | 5 | ST0284 | 1392 | 6.19 | | 711 | ST0145 | 1335 | 10.5 | | 198 | ST0677 | 1174 | 8.34 | | 486 | ST0129 | 1052 | 8.21 | | 640 | ST0202 | 1051 | 5.05 | | 82 | ST0344 | 808 | 7.96 | | 489 | ST0167 | 629 | 10.09 | | 224 | ST0655 | 283 | 8.33 | ::: ::: ::: All 10 lie between 283 and 1581 m, about ten times a normal shelf depth, and their temperatures fit stations a tenth as deep. Dividing by ten is a correction with evidence behind it, not a convenience: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} clean <- clean |> mutate(depth_m = if_else(depth_m > 250, depth_m / 10, depth_m)) range(clean$depth_m) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] 5.0 194.6 ``` ::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} clean["depth_m"] = clean["depth_m"].where( clean["depth_m"] <= 250, clean["depth_m"] / 10 ) clean["depth_m"].agg(["min", "max"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> min 5.0 #> max 194.6 #> Name: depth_m, dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: ::: A correction that makes the data fit expectations is also how confirmation bias works. State the rule, apply it to every row, and report how many rows it changed. ## An instrument offset shifts every reading The salinity offset between the two vessels is neither missing nor an outlier: it shifts every reading one vessel took. Correct it against a calibration record if one exists, or give the model `vessel` as a feature so it can learn the offset. ## Dropping incomplete rows deletes winter Most modelling functions silently drop any row with a missing value. Here is what that costs: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} comparison <- bind_rows( clean |> count(season) |> mutate(dataset = "All rows"), clean |> drop_na() |> count(season) |> mutate(dataset = "Complete rows only") ) ggplot(comparison, aes(season, n, fill = dataset)) + geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), width = 0.68) + geom_text(aes(label = n), position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.4) + scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) + labs(x = NULL, y = "Stations", fill = NULL, title = "Where the dropped rows come from") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Stations per season before and after dropping every row with a missing value. Winter loses far more than the other seasons, so the data becomes less wintry than the survey that produced it.](missing-values-and-outliers_files/figure-html/fig-deletion-1.png){#fig-deletion fig-alt='Grouped bar chart of stations per season, with all rows and with complete cases only. Autumn, spring and summer barely change, while winter drops visibly.' width=1500} ::: ::: Dropping incomplete rows loses 10% of the stations overall, but 20% of winter. A question about winter conditions has just lost a large part of its evidence, without a warning. ## Filling gaps belongs inside the model The alternative is **imputation**: predicting each missing value from the columns that were recorded. The `recipes` package has steps for it, such as `step_impute_median()` and `step_impute_knn()`, and [Scaling and encoding](scaling-and-encoding.qmd) puts them into a recipe. Two rules apply: - **Impute as part of the model, not beforehand.** Filling gaps with the average of the whole dataset lets the data that will test the model shape the data that trains it; [Avoiding information leakage](information-leakage.qmd) explains why that matters. - **An imputed value is a guess, not a measurement.** A column recording which values were filled in lets the model, and you, see where the gaps were. Imputation cannot create information that was never collected: winter chlorophyll will stay less certain than summer's whatever method is used. And every choice on this page changes the results, so each belongs in the methods section of a paper. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - Ask why a value is missing: gaps that follow a recorded column can be filled in; gaps that depend on the missing value itself cannot. - Impossible values are corrected or marked missing; genuine extremes are kept, however far from the average. - Convert sentinel values such as −999 to missing values before any summary. - Dropping incomplete rows is a silent default, and here it removes far more of winter than of any other season. - Impute as part of the model, and keep a record of which values were filled in. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Compare `step_impute_median()` with `step_impute_knn()` for chlorophyll. How different are the filled-in winter values? 2. If cloud causes the missing chlorophyll, and cloud also lowers chlorophyll, which kind of missing value is it? Could any imputation method fix it?
